name: Kunthunatha
summary: Jains revere Kunthunatha as the 17th Tirthankara of this age, born in Hastinapur and counted as a world-emperor. His emblem is a goat and his name recalls a heap of jewels.
about: According to Jain tradition, Kunthunatha was born in Hastinapur to King Sura and Queen Shri of the Ikshvaku line. Svetambara texts say his name came from a dream in which his mother saw a heap of jewels, called kunthu. Jain tradition also counts him as the sixth chakravartin, a ruler of the whole earth, and the twelfth kamadeva. After a long reign he renounced his empire, wandered as an ascetic for sixteen years, reached omniscience and taught a large community. Jains believe he attained liberation on Mount Shikharji. Svetambara and Digambara sources differ in his parents' names and in several figures. His temples range from Hampi to Jaisalmer.
kidSummary: Kunthunatha is remembered by Jains as the 17th Tirthankara. His name is linked to a dream of a shining heap of jewels, and his sign is a goat. The stories say he ruled the whole earth and then gave it up to seek peace.

story.title: A dream of jewels
story.text: Svetambara texts say his mother dreamed of a glittering heap of gems called kunthu. The baby was named after that dream.

story.title: Ruler of the earth
story.text: He grew up in Hastinapur and became king. Jain accounts say a divine wheel appeared in his armoury and the kings of the land accepted his rule without a battle.

story.title: Names on the mountain
story.text: Among the stories told of Jain world-emperors, he saw the names of earlier emperors carved at a mountain foot. That helped him realise that even great power is only temporary.

story.title: A long, quiet search
story.text: He gave up his throne and joined a thousand kings as an ascetic. Jain texts say he meditated for sixteen years before he gained perfect knowledge under a tilaka tree.

story.title: The final fast
story.text: He taught about purity of the mind. At the end, Jains believe, he fasted for a month on Mount Shikharji and reached liberation.

facts.text: Jainpedia says the name Kunthu is unclear and may not even be Sanskrit. Svetambara texts tie it to a heap of jewels in his mother's dream, while one commentary reads it as 'staying on the earth'.
A divine disc appeared in his armoury, and Jainworld says he won the world without a battle, since every king accepted his rule.
Wikipedia retells a legend, told of every chakravartin, that he went to carve his name on a mountain foot, found earlier emperors' names already there, felt his ambition shrink and renounced.
Jainworld says he took initiation together with 1,000 kings and at once gained manahparyaya, the knowledge of other minds' thoughts.
A hoard of 11th-century Digambara bronzes found at Aluara near Dhanbad, Jharkhand, includes rare idols of Kunthunatha seated in lotus posture. They are now kept at the Patna Museum.
Karanthai in Tamil Nadu, also called Munigiri, has a 9th-century Pallava-era inscription. Under the Cholas its Kunthunatha temple carried a king's name, Virarajendrapperumpalli.
The Ganigitti Jain temple at Hampi was built in 1385 under the Vijayanagara Empire by the commander Iruguppa. An inscription dedicates its main shrine to Kunthunatha.
Jain texts give him 95,000 years of life and a height of 35 bows. At about three metres a bow, the usual conversion, that is roughly 105 metres tall.

quiz.q: What does Svetambara tradition say inspired the name Kunthu?
quiz.why: His mother dreamed of a heap of jewels called kunthu.
A goat is carved on the base of his images.

quiz.q: Besides being a Tirthankara, what do Jain texts call him?
quiz.why: Jain tradition counts him as the sixth chakravartin, a world-emperor.

quiz.q: Where is his birthplace in Jain tradition?
quiz.why: Jain tradition places his birth at Hastinapur, near Meerut.

quiz.q: How many years did he wander before omniscience?
quiz.why: Jain texts say he wandered as an ascetic for 16 years.
